items.prose: You must drop every negative P&L entry from `std::vector<double> pnl`.
items.question: Which loop is correct?

options.text: `for (auto it = pnl.begin(); it != pnl.end(); ) { if (*it < 0) it = pnl.erase(it); else ++it; }`
`for (auto it = pnl.begin(); it != pnl.end(); ++it) { if (*it < 0) pnl.erase(it); }`
options.why: After `erase`, `it` is invalid, and `++it` skips the element that slid into its place.

options.text: `for (std::size_t i = 0; i < pnl.size(); ++i) { if (pnl[i] < 0) pnl.erase(pnl.begin() + i); }`
options.why: After erasing at `i`, the next element moves to `i`, and `++i` skips it. Two negatives in a row leave one behind.

feedback.correct: Take the iterator `erase` returns, and step only when you keep the element.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the loop over two negatives in a row.

explain.text: `erase` shifts later elements left and returns an iterator to the next one. Stepping only when you did not erase visits every element once. `pnl.erase(std::remove_if(...), pnl.end())` does the same with algorithms.

items.prose: A tool counts trades per symbol over a day, then prints one line per symbol in alphabetical order.
items.question: Which container fits?

options.why: It counts fine, but its loop order follows the hash. You would have to sort the keys before printing.
A vector is indexed by number; symbols are text.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which container keeps its keys sorted?

explain.text: A `std::map` keeps keys sorted, so one loop prints them in order. A few thousand symbols cost about a dozen comparisons each.

items.question: What is `total`?

feedback.correct: 8: the total is an `int` and drops each half.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the running total as an `int` after every addition.

byKey.ten: You summed exactly. The start value `0` makes the total an `int`: 2, 4, 6, 8.

explain.text: Each step computes `int + double`, then stores it back in an `int`. So 2.5 becomes 2, then 4.5 becomes 4, and so on. Start at `0.0` to get 10.

items.prose: Asks queue by price, lowest first, then by time, earliest first. `Order` has `price` and `time`.
items.question: Which comparator sorts them?

options.text: `[](const Order& a, const Order& b) { return a.price != b.price ? a.price < b.price : a.time < b.time; }`
`[](const Order& a, const Order& b) { return a.price <= b.price; }`
options.why: `<=` is not strict, and it ignores time. Equal prices answer true both ways, which breaks `sort`.

options.text: `[](const Order& a, const Order& b) { return a.price != b.price ? a.price > b.price : a.time < b.time; }`
options.why: `>` puts the highest price first. That is the order for bids, not asks.

options.text: `[](const Order& a, const Order& b) { return a.time < b.time; }`
options.why: That sorts by time alone, ignoring price.

feedback.correct: Price first, time on a tie, both strict.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which rule puts the lowest price first and breaks ties by time?

explain.text: For asks the best price is the lowest, so price uses `<`; a tie falls back to the earlier time. Both comparisons are strict, as `sort` requires.

items.prose:
`cmake --build build` compiles every file, then stops:

```text
undefined reference to `vwap(std::vector<double> const&, std::vector<double> const&)'
```
`vwap` lives in the `pricing` library, used by the target `tests`.
items.question: Which line fixes it?

options.why: Every file compiled, so the headers were found. The linker is missing the code.
A missing standard shows up as compile errors, not as an undefined reference.
Nothing has changed, so the same link fails the same way.

feedback.correct: An undefined reference means a missing link.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which step failed: compiling or linking?

explain.text: Compiling needs declarations; linking needs the code. `target_link_libraries` joins `pricing` to `tests`, and passes on its public include folder too.

items.prose: Put the lines of a test in arrange, act, assert order.
items.question: Order the lines.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Inputs first, then the one call, then the checks.

explain.text: The test sets up the closes, calls the code once and then checks the result. The two checks can go in either order; both describe the one behaviour.

items.prose: A test reads `CHECK(vwap({10.1, 10.2}, {1, 1}) == 10.15);` and fails on correct code.
items.question: What is the fix?

options.text: Round `vwap`'s result to two places inside `vwap`
options.why: That changes the code to suit a bad test, and loses precision for every caller.

options.text: Delete the test, since the code is right
options.why: The behaviour still needs a test. Compare with a tolerance instead.
A `float` rounds more, not less. The fix is in the comparison.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Why might the exact `==` fail on correct code?

explain.text: In doubles, (10.1 + 10.2) / 2 comes out as 10.149999999999999, not the `double` nearest 10.15. A tolerance of `1e-9` absorbs that and still catches real errors.
